newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nabs smugglers amid tide of Chinese illegals.
newsitem.headline: Japan nabs smugglers amid tide of Chinese illegals.

text.p: Police have arrested seven Chinese suspected of leading a Japan-based "Snakehead" immigrant smuggling ring, the first major salvo in Japan's fight against a rising number of illegal Chinese aliens.

The seven were arrested along with 10 others on suspicion of violating immigration laws for smuggling 70 Chinese into Japan, where long, sparsely populated coasts and high wages have drawn record numbers of Chinese this year, police said on Thursday.

The 581 Chinese nationals caught as of February 24 tops the record 545 detained last year, and those caught could represent as few as one-tenth of those who successfully sneak into Japan, officials warned.
Investigations and testimony by the would-be immigrants reveals an increasingly sophisticated Chinese smuggling network inside Japan, Japan's top police official said.

"The Snakehead broker groups have made inroads in Japan and are increasingly active here," Takaji Kunimatsu, head of the National Police Agency, told a news conference. "We are proceeding to uncover more about their organisation."
The network uses fake travel documents and employs a fleet of small boats with ultra-modern navigation equipment to evade maritime patrols, police said.

They lure people from Fujian Province and other densely-populated coastal Chinese provinces with the promise of high-paying factory jobs, typically charging 3 million yen ($24,700) for the passage, would-be immigrants have said.

The arrest this week of the Japan-based Snakeheads -- secretive gangs so called for their viciousness -- suggests that the Chinese smugglers are bypassing Japanese gangsters to set up routes between China and Japan, officials said.
Tokyo resident Zhang Shiyi, 27, was in police custody and suspected of leading a Chinese underground group that smuggles Chinese aliens, police said.

Zhang and two other suspected ringleaders are accused of brokering the illegal entry of about 70 Chinese into Japan via the southernmost prefecture of Okinawa last December. Only nine of those Chinese were caught.

The arrest of Zhang and his cohorts is the latest of a series of seizures of large groups of Chinese nationals atempting to illegally enter Japan, where wages are many times higher than in China and other Asian countries.

On Sunday, Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) officials seized the 200-tonne "Johaiyu" with 51 Chinese -- 44 men and 7 women -- on board. The 51 and three Japanese were arrested the next day on illegal immigration charges.

On Tuesday, police in the western city of Matsue arrested 55 men from Bangladesh, Pakistan and Iran for illegally entering the country. The men told investigators they travelled to Japan from the South Korean port of Pusan.

The tide of Chinese illegal immigrants, which has sparked worries of increasing inter-Chinese crimes after several killings and other violent attacks, prompted Japan's Foreign Ministry to ask Beijing to crack down on the traffic.
Immigration officials say they cannot explain the sudden surge in illegal immigration to Japan, where the job market has tightened after a prolonged recession.

Japanese media reports have suggested that Japan, with thousands of islands and long coast, has been targetted by the Snakeheads because of a slower economy in Taiwan and uncertainty about Hong Kong with the approach of British colony's return to Chinese sovereignty in July.
